title: Renderer comparison
description: How the four chart backends differ, which one your browser runs, and how they compare on this device: live benchmarks with frame rates, frame times, main-thread cost, startup and a score out of 100.

chain.title: How a chart picks its backend
chain.text: Cartesian charts (line, area, bar, scatter, candlestick, heatmap, sparkline, quadrant) draw their data with one of four backends and their text (axes, labels, legend, tooltip) with the DOM. All four draw the same marks with the same colors; they differ in speed, startup cost, availability and limits.
chain.auto: renderer="auto" (default) tries WebGPU, then WebGL2, then WebGL, then Canvas2D, and keeps the first one that starts. onRendererChange, the renderer event and the ready promise report the backend in use.
chain.software: Auto skips GPUs that run in software (SwiftShader, llvmpipe, Microsoft Basic Render Driver…): they are slower than Canvas2D, so virtual machines and headless browsers usually end up on Canvas2D.
chain.forced: renderer="webgpu" | "webgl2" | "webgl" | "canvas2d" forces a backend, software GPUs included. If it cannot start, the chart moves down the chain, never up.
chain.lost: When the GPU is lost (driver reset, device removed, context evicted), the chart moves to the next backend, redraws with the same data, zoom and state, and reports the new backend.
chain.global: setDefaultChartRenderer() sets the backend of every chart whose renderer is unset or "auto", in React, Vue, Angular and Web Components; charts on screen switch live.

matrix.title: At a glance
matrix.text: What each backend uses underneath, how it draws a frame and where its limits are.

api.label: Browser API
api.webgpu: WebGPU, on top of Vulkan, Metal or Direct3D 12
api.webgl: WebGL 1.0 (OpenGL ES 2.0) with the ANGLE_instanced_arrays extension
api.canvas2d: The Canvas 2D context, rasterized by the browser

shaders.label: Shaders
shaders.canvas2d: None: paths, rectangles and pixels drawn from JavaScript

draw.label: Drawing a frame
draw.webgpu: One instanced draw per series from GPU buffers
draw.webgl2: One instanced draw per series, one vertex array per series
draw.webgl: One instanced draw per series, attributes bound again for each draw (no vertex arrays)
draw.canvas2d: Every visible mark is drawn again by JavaScript

zoom.label: Zoom and pan
zoom.webgpu: Only a transform changes: no buffer is rebuilt
zoom.webgl2: Only a transform changes: no buffer is rebuilt
zoom.webgl: Only a transform changes: no buffer is rebuilt
zoom.canvas2d: The visible range is drawn again on each frame

lines.label: Millions of line points
lines.canvas2d: Decimated to the min / max of each pixel column (at most 4 points per column), same silhouette

scatter.label: Large scatter sets
scatter.webgpu: Every dot, one instanced draw per series
scatter.webgl2: Every dot, one instanced draw per series
scatter.webgl: Every dot, one instanced draw per series
scatter.canvas2d: Above 20,000 points, written pixel by pixel into an ImageData buffer: still O(n) per frame

contexts.label: Contexts per page
contexts.webgpu: One device per chart; not counted in the WebGL limit
contexts.webgl2: Browsers keep about 16 live WebGL contexts: past that, off-screen charts are suspended and restored when they scroll back
contexts.webgl: Same limit as WebGL2, shared with it

start.label: Startup
start.webgl2: Synchronous context, shaders compiled at start
start.webgl: Synchronous context, shaders compiled at start

fit.label: Best for
fit.webgpu: Millions of points, live data, long zoom sessions
fit.webgl2: The same workloads where WebGPU is missing; the most widely available fast path
fit.webgl: Older GPUs, drivers and browsers without WebGL2
fit.canvas2d: Small charts, many charts per page, software GPUs, no GPU at all

expect.title: What to expect
expect.text: Trends from the measurements below, not promises: run the benchmarks on this page to measure your device.
expect.small: Up to tens of thousands of points, every backend keeps up with the display; Canvas2D needs no GPU context at all.
expect.medium: Lines and areas: Canvas2D decimates them to the pixel columns, so even 2 million sorted points stay smooth on a fast CPU, and the GPU backends cost about the same whatever the size.
expect.large: Scatter sets are where the backends part ways: Canvas2D draws every dot on every frame, so its main-thread time grows with the dots (about 8 ms at 100K, 12 ms at 1M and 21 ms at 2M on the sample machine, where it drops below the refresh rate), while the GPU backends stay around 1 to 3 ms.
expect.bars: Bars: up to 200K bars every backend kept up on the sample machine, the GPU backends with the least main-thread time.
expect.gpus: WebGPU, WebGL2 and WebGL are often within a millisecond or two of each other, about the size of the run-to-run noise. Integrated graphics, older GPUs and phones widen the gaps; slower CPUs make Canvas2D fall behind sooner.
expect.startup: The first frame takes tens of milliseconds and grows with the data to upload (about 100 ms for 2 million dots on the sample machine).

sample.title: Sample results
sample.text: One run of the benchmark demo on an Apple M3 Max laptop, Chrome 156 on macOS, 60 Hz display, pixel ratio 1, 3 s per backend. Each cell gives the score and the main-thread time per frame, plus the frame rate when it fell below the display's.
sample.note: Numbers from one machine and one run: differences of a few points or a millisecond are within the noise. Run the benchmark above to get your own.

score.title: How the score is computed
score.text: Each run ends with a score out of 100, computed only from what was measured, relative to this display's refresh rate (measured before the run). Four parts, each between 0 and 1:
score.smooth: Smoothness (40%): frames per second divided by the refresh rate.
score.stability: Stability (20%): the frame budget (1000 ms / refresh rate) divided by the 95th percentile frame interval, so long frames cost points even when the average is fine.
score.headroom: Headroom (25%): one minus the main-thread time of a frame divided by the frame budget, i.e. how much of each frame is left for your application.
score.startup: Startup (15%): one minus the time from mounting the chart to its first painted frame divided by one second.
score.grades: Grades: 85 and above excellent, 65 and above good, 40 and above fair, below 40 poor. A score compares backends on one device and one workload; it is not comparable across machines.

method.title: Methodology and caveats
method.text: The benchmark mounts one chart at a time, forced onto a backend, with the same data and the same camera path:
method.same: Data: seeded typed-array columns generated once before the clock starts and shared by every backend. The camera zooms from the whole data set (the heaviest frame) to the deepest zoom and back while drifting sideways, with setView on every animation frame.
method.work: Main-thread time: from the start of an animation frame to a message posted in it, which runs once the frame is rendered; it includes the chart's JavaScript and draw calls, style, layout and paint.
method.vsync: Frame rates are capped by the display: two backends at the refresh rate tie on smoothness and differ in headroom.
method.gpu: GPU time after the draw calls is not visible to JavaScript: a backend that submits quickly but saturates the GPU shows it through a lower frame rate and longer frame intervals.
method.noise: Results vary with power mode, thermal throttling, other tabs and browser extensions. Keep the tab in front during a run, and run it twice to compare.

browsers.title: Browser support
browsers.text: Where each backend is available. Versions are the first stable releases with the feature on by default; support also depends on the GPU and its driver.
browsers.note: WebGPU only runs in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost). Browsers block some GPUs and drivers, in which case the chart falls back automatically. The Your device demo above shows what this browser actually offers.

firefox.label: Firefox (desktop)
firefox.webgpu: 141+ on Windows; other platforms rolling out

linux.label: Chrome on Linux
linux.webgpu: Depends on the version and the GPU driver

choose.title: Which one to use
choose.auto: Leave renderer on "auto" in production: every visitor gets the fastest backend their device runs in hardware, and losses are handled for you.
choose.webgpu: Force WebGPU only to test it or to compare it; auto already picks it first when it runs in hardware.
choose.webgl2: Force WebGL2 when a WebGPU driver misbehaves on the devices you target, or to keep identical rendering across browsers that ship WebGPU at different times.
choose.webgl: Force WebGL to reproduce what older devices see.
choose.canvas2d: Force Canvas2D for small charts, thumbnails and sparklines, for pages with dozens of charts (no context limit), and for environments without a GPU.
choose.many: A dashboard with many charts: keep the large or interactive ones on auto and put the small ones on Canvas2D, or destroy the charts that leave the screen.
choose.more: Data formats, streaming and the million-point showcases are on <performance>Chart performance</performance>; the framework-free API is on <engine>Chart engine</engine>.

env.noInstancing: no instancing: falls back to Canvas2D

examples.title: Benchmark and score
examples.description: Pick a workload (line, scatter or bars), a size and a duration, then run: each backend draws the same data under the same zoom path, one after the other. The table gives the frame rate, median and 95th percentile frame times, main-thread time per frame and time to first frame; the cards and the bars give the score and its parts. Copy the results as a Markdown table to share them.

examples.title: Your device
examples.description: Probes each backend the way the engine does: whether it starts on a hardware GPU, on a software one or not at all, the GPU and API versions the browser reports, a few limits, and the backend renderer="auto" picks here. Every probe releases its context right away.

examples.title: Losing the GPU
examples.description: Simulates a GPU loss on the backend in use (WEBGL_lose_context for WebGL, destroying the device for WebGPU): the chart moves to the next backend and redraws, down to Canvas2D. The log shows how long each recovery took.

examples.title: Scaling with the number of points
examples.description: Runs every hardware backend at 10K, 100K, 1M and 2M points (1.5 s each) and plots the frame rate and the main-thread time per frame against the size, on log axes: the GPU curves stay flat where Canvas2D climbs.

examples.title: Switching backends live
examples.description: The renderer prop changes the backend of a chart on screen: it recreates its renderer in place and keeps its data and zoom. The log shows the backend drawn and how long it took to start; a forced backend that cannot start moves down the chain. Auto follows the renderer bar at the top of the page.

snippets.source:
const budget = 1000 / refreshRate; // ms per frame: 16.7 at 60 Hz

const smooth = clamp(fps / refreshRate); // keeps up with the display
const stability = clamp(budget / p95FrameTime); // no long frames
const headroom = clamp(1 - mainThreadPerFrame / budget); // CPU left for the app
const startup = clamp(1 - timeToFirstFrame / 1000); // chart on screen quickly

const score = Math.round(
  100 * (0.4 * smooth + 0.2 * stability + 0.25 * headroom + 0.15 * startup),
); // clamp: between 0 and 1
